query: For an FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy protective coating susceptible to progressive plastic deformation during continuous loading, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain its creep resistance? Specify the governing factor and rationale, an unspecified controlled comparison that would reveal it, predicted observations relative to the starting baseline, the operating boundaries under sustained stress, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Thermal processing designed to refine and increase the density of FCC/BCC interphase boundaries in the dual‐phase high-entropy alloy protective coating will enhance its creep resistance under sustained loading by more effectively impeding dislocation motion.
generation.material_initial_state: A protective coating with a dual‐phase FCC/BCC microstructure obtained by standard processing, featuring relatively diffuse or less optimally distributed interphase boundaries.
generation.intervention: Apply controlled thermal processing (e.g., annealing or post-deposition heat treatment) to modify and sharpen the FCC/BCC interfaces.
generation.conditions: Continuous uniaxial loading at moderately high temperatures (within the phase-stable range, e.g., below 800°C) representative of service conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Sharpened and refined FCC/BCC interphase boundaries that serve as obstacles to dislocation motion.
generation.mechanism: Refined interphase boundaries more effectively pin dislocations in the FCC matrix, thereby increasing the effective stress required for dislocation climb or glide and consequently reducing the creep strain rate.
generation.predicted_outcome: Coatings subjected to controlled thermal processing will exhibit a lower secondary creep strain rate and higher stress exponent compared to the as-deposited baseline, with microstructural analyses revealing enhanced dislocation pile-up or pinning at the optimized interfaces.
generation.baseline: The as-deposited dual‐phase coating with standard interphase boundary characteristics.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is anticipated to hold under sustained mechanical loading at temperatures that preserve phase stability; variations outside these conditions may invoke other deformation mechanisms.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative improvement in creep resistance and the degree of dislocation impediment achievable through interface sharpening remain to be precisely determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of dual-phase high-entropy alloy protective coating samples: one set processed by standard deposition (baseline) and another set subjected to controlled thermal processing aimed at refining the FCC/BCC interface. Subject both sets to constant uniaxial stress at a moderate temperature (e.g., below 800°C), and conduct in situ and post-mortem microstructural characterization using electron microscopy alongside mechanical creep testing.
measurements: Creep strain rate and stress exponent from constant-load creep tests
Quantitative imaging of FCC/BCC interface sharpness and density via TEM/EBSD
Observation of dislocation accumulation and pinning at interphase boundaries
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the thermally processed coatings do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in creep strain rate (or increase in stress exponent) relative to the baseline, or if microstructural analyses do not show enhanced dislocation obstruction at FCC/BCC boundaries, then the hypothesized mechanism is falsified.

AlxCr0.2NbTiV (x = 0.2, 0.5, or 0.8) refractory high-entropy alloys were fabricated by arc melting. The effects of Al content on the microstructure of AlxCr0.2NbTiV alloys were studied using X-ray diffraction, scanning electron microscopy, and electron backscatter diffraction. The microhardness, compression properties, and nanoindentation creep properties of AlxCr0.2NbTiV alloys were also tested. AbstractMulti‐principal element alloys (MPEA) demonstrate exceptional stability during rapid solidification, making them ideal candidates for additive manufacturing and other high‐design‐flexibility techniques. Unexpectedly, MPEA failure often mimics that of conventional metals, with strain localization along phase or grain boundaries leading to typical crack initiation. Most strategies aim at reducing strain localization either suppress the formation of high‐energy sites or dissipate energy at crack tips to enhance toughness, rarely achieving a synergy of both. Inspired by the microstructure of mouse enamel, nanoscale body‐centered cubic (BCC) and face‐centered cubic (FCC) phases into MPEAs are introduced, stabilized at phase boundaries to provide ample plastic space for dislocation‐mediated deformation. This approach overcomes the local hardening limitations of nanoscale alloys and harmonizes traditional toughening mechanisms—such as crack deflection, blocking, and bridging—to mitigate strain localization. AbstractIn aero-engine applications, turbine blades operate under high-temperature and high-pressure thermomechanical cyclic loading conditions, which demand exceptional mechanical performance. High-entropy superalloys, characterized by a stable dual-phase γ/γ′ microstructure, have emerged as promising candidates for high-temperature structural materials due to their superior creep resistance. In this study, the creep behaviors of high-entropy superalloys are systematically investigated using molecular dynamics simulations, exploring the effects of stress, temperature, γ/γ′ lattice misfit, and γ′ volume fraction on creep deformation mechanisms. The results show that both stress and temperature significantly influence creep behavior, with temperature exerting a more dominant effect. As the applied stress increases, the dominant creep mechanism evolves from atomic diffusion to dislocation nucleation and motion, eventually leading to phase transformation. Additionally, the γ/γ′ lattice misfit and γ′ volume fraction are found to critically affect the alloy’s creep resistance. AbstractA face-centered-cubic (fcc) oriented FeCoCrNiAl0.5 dual-phase high entropy alloy (HEA) was plastically strained in uniaxial compression at 77K and 293K and the underlying deformation mechanisms were studied. The undeformed microstructure consists of a body-centered-cubic (bcc)/B2 interdendritic network and precipitates embedded in 〈001〉-oriented fcc dendrites. In contrast to other dual-phase HEAs, at both deformation temperatures a steep rise in the stress-strain curves occurs above 23% total axial strain. As a result, the hardening rate associated saturates at the unusual high value of ~6 GPa. Analysis of the strain partitioning between fcc and bcc/B2 by digital image correlation shows that the fcc component carries the larger part of the plastic strain. Further, electron backscatter diffraction and transmission electron microscopy evidence ample fcc deformation twinning both at 77K and 293K, while slip activity only is found in the bcc/B2. These results may guide future advancements in the design of novel alloys with superior toughening characteristics.

cited_evidence.kind: web:The promise of dual-phase high entropy alloys
cited_evidence.text: The material studied here is a FeCoCrNiAl0.5 alloy, characterized by a two-phase microstructure consisting of 〈001〉-oriented fcc dendrites with fine bcc/B2 precipitates embedded and bounded by a bcc/B2 interdendritic. The intimate two-phase fcc + bcc/B2 microstructure is expected to entail complex heterogeneous strain partitioning between these phases because of their mechanical contrast. Also, heterogeneous grain and phase distributions in addition to segregations (chemical gradients) resulting from the dendritic solidification during casting add to the intricacy of its stress-strain response. Our experiments reveal that this composition shows exceptional work hardening both at 293K and 77K, considerably higher than previously reported hardening rates for e.g. Fe-Mn and Hadfield steels,. Based on the experimental observations elaborated below we attribute the substantial hardening to the combined action of these 3 contributions: (i) the fcc – bcc/B2 interphase boundaries resulting from the dendritic-interdendritic microstructure, (ii) extensive deformation twinning in fcc, (iii) fine and dense bcc/B2 precipitates inside the fcc dendrites.

In this section we present the key experimental observations documenting the stress-strain response of dual-phase FeCoCrNiAl0.5 in relation to its pristine vs. deformed microstructure. After characterizing the undeformed microstructure by EBSD and TEM, the influence of temperature (293K vs. 77K) on the strain-hardening rate is studied and the strain partitioning between fcc and bcc/B2 determined from DIC strain maps. EBSD and (high-resolution) TEM of deformed FeCoCrNiAl0.5 reveal deformation twinning in the fcc phase.

In the present study, the tensile creep tests under constant stress were performed on multiple fine-grained CoCrFeNiMn HEA specimens in the temperature range of 500–600 °C. Specifically, some tests were interrupted at the steady-state stages and cooled quickly to reserve the crept microstructures for examining the microstructural evolution. The objective was to reveal the inherent relationship between microstructural evolution and creep properties of single-phase CoCrFeNiMn high-entropy alloy.

drafts.hypothesis: Creep resistance in the FCC/BCC high-entropy alloy coating is primarily governed by the ability of sharply defined FCC/BCC interphase boundaries to pin dislocations under sustained loading, thereby mitigating progressive plastic deformation.
drafts.material_initial_state: An as-deposited FCC/BCC high-entropy alloy protective coating with naturally occurring interphase boundaries between the FCC and BCC regions.
drafts.intervention: Subject samples to sustained constant stress at moderate temperatures, while also preparing a controlled comparison set where the interface sharpness is altered via a post-deposition heat treatment.
drafts.conditions: Tests performed under continuous loading at temperatures within the phase-stability window (moderate temperatures well below transformation limits) and stresses below the yield limit such that creep deformation is the dominant mechanism.
drafts.structural_mediator: The sharp FCC/BCC interphase boundaries that act as obstacles to dislocation motion.
drafts.mechanism: Under sustained stress, dislocations accumulate and are pinned at the phase boundaries. Sharper, more defined boundaries enhance this pinning effect, limiting dislocation glide and thus reducing creep rate compared to coatings with more diffuse interfaces.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Samples with heat-treated, sharper interfaces will show a measurable decrease in creep rates (or longer time to reach a given strain) relative to the baseline as-deposited samples. Microstructural analysis will reveal a higher density of pinned dislocations at the interfaces in the enhanced samples.
drafts.baseline: The as-deposited coating exhibiting the standard microstructural interphase characteristics, with a known creep rate under the specified loading conditions.
drafts.boundary: The hypothesis is expected to be valid under stress conditions that do not induce phase transformations or other instability phenomena; it applies for sustained stress and temperature conditions within the phase-stable range of the alloy.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of coating specimens: one set with the as-deposited microstructure and one set subjected to a controlled heat treatment designed to sharpen the FCC/BCC interfaces. Conduct constant-load creep tests under identical moderate temperature conditions while monitoring creep strain over time.
measurements: Creep rate (slope of strain vs. time curves)
Microstructural characterization (e.g., TEM imaging) of the interface regions to assess dislocation pinning
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the heat-treated specimens with sharper interfaces do not show a statistically significant reduction in creep rate (or an increase in time to failure) compared to the as-deposited specimens, or if there is no evidence of increased dislocation pinning at the interfaces in the treated samples, then the hypothesis should be rejected.

drafts.hypothesis: The creep resistance of the FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy protective coating is governed by its dual-phase microstructure, where the BCC phase acts as a barrier to dislocation motion in the FCC matrix. This interaction at the FCC/BCC interfaces causes enhanced dislocation crowding and impeding sliding under continuous loading, thereby reducing the creep rate relative to a comparable single-phase alloy.
drafts.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy coating with a dual-phase microstructure (containing both FCC and BCC phases) exhibiting a uniform phase distribution and minimal dislocation density after proper annealing.
drafts.intervention: Subject the coating to prolonged creep testing at sustained high temperatures and mechanical loads that simulate service conditions.
drafts.conditions: Creep tests conducted under constant load and temperature conditions, with a controlled comparison between the dual-phase alloy and a variant with a single-phase microstructure (prepared via rapid quenching to suppress phase separation).
drafts.structural_mediator: The FCC/BCC phase interfaces that provide obstacles to dislocation motion and promote dislocation hardening.
drafts.mechanism: Under sustained stress, dislocations are generated in the FCC matrix but are impeded at the FCC/BCC interfaces. The BCC phase serves as an effective barrier, causing dislocation pile-up and delaying their glide. In contrast, a single-phase alloy would allow more unobstructed dislocation flow, leading to faster creep.
drafts.predicted_outcome: The dual-phase coating is predicted to exhibit a lower secondary creep rate and accumulate less plastic strain over time compared to the single-phase variant. Microstructural analysis should show increased dislocation density localizing near the phase interfaces in the dual-phase sample.
drafts.baseline: The initial mechanical and microstructural state of the dual-phase high-entropy alloy coating, as well as the corresponding data from a single-phase control sample prepared under similar conditions.
drafts.boundary: The hypothesis is expected to hold under sustained high-temperature and high-stress conditions relevant to service. Deviations in temperature, stress level or non-representative phase distributions could alter the observed behavior.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct parallel creep tests on the dual-phase coating and a single-phase variant under identical mechanical and thermal conditions. Use TEM and SEM to examine and compare dislocation structures and phase boundary interactions before and after creep testing.
measurements: Total accumulated plastic strain over a fixed period
Phase volume fractions and potential evolution during creep
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the dual-phase high-entropy alloy does not exhibit a statistically significant lower creep rate and reduced accumulated strain compared to the single-phase counterpart, or if microstructural analysis fails to show enhanced dislocation blockage at the phase interfaces, then the hypothesis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: The exceptional creep resistance of the dual‐phase FCC/BCC protective coating is primarily governed by the synergistic effect of coherent FCC/BCC interfaces. These interfaces promote deformation twinning in the FCC phase and serve as effective barriers to dislocation glide and diffusion in the BCC phase, thereby delaying progressive plastic deformation under continuous loading.
drafts.material_initial_state: A protective coating with a dual‐phase microstructure consisting of 〈001〉‐oriented FCC dendrites interpenetrated by fine, coherent BCC/B2 precipitates or interdendritic regions.
drafts.intervention: Modify the interphase (FCC/BCC) boundary density via controlled thermal processing (or annealing) to alter precipitate size and distribution.
drafts.conditions: Sustained mechanical loading at elevated temperatures (e.g., in the range where dislocation creep and deformation twinning are active) similar to service conditions for protective coatings.
drafts.structural_mediator: The coherent interfaces between FCC and BCC phases which, by virtue of their high density and spatial arrangement, mediate strain partitioning and inhibit dislocation motion and vacancy diffusion.
drafts.mechanism: Under continuous loading, the FCC phase undergoes deformation twinning that enhances strain hardening, while the BCC phase—with its fine, coherent precipitates—obstructs dislocation glide and retards lattice diffusion. The interaction between these two mechanisms at the interphase boundaries effectively delays tertiary creep and plastic degradation.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Coatings with a higher density of coherent FCC/BCC interfaces (i.e., finer BCC precipitates and stronger interphase bonding) will demonstrate a lower steady‐state creep rate and a longer creep rupture life compared to coatings in which these interfaces are coarsened or less coherent.
drafts.baseline: The as-deposited protective coating exhibiting its standard dual-phase architecture with the known FCC dendrites and BCC/B2 regions.
drafts.boundary: This mechanism is expected to operate under sustained high temperature and stress conditions where both dislocation-controlled creep and deformation twinning are active; outside these regimes, other mechanisms (e.g., diffusion creep) might dominate.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of coatings with identical overall compositions: one set processed to maintain a fine, high-density FCC/BCC interphase boundary structure and a second set subjected to a thermal treatment designed to coarsen the BCC precipitates (reducing interface density). Subject both sets to identical sustained loading tests at elevated temperatures and measure the creep rate and creep rupture life.
measurements: Microstructural characterization of phase boundary density (via EBSD/TEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the sample with coarsened BCC precipitates (lower interface density) does not exhibit a significantly higher steady-state creep rate and reduced creep life compared to the standard dual-phase coating, then the hypothesis that the coherent FCC/BCC interfaces govern the creep resistance is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: In FCC/BCC dual-phase high-entropy protective coatings, enhanced creep resistance under continuous loading is achieved by a dynamic interaction between the FCC matrix and dispersed BCC precipitates at the interphase boundaries. The BCC precipitates act as barriers to dislocation climb and diffusion-controlled deformation, while the FCC regions accommodate plastic deformation through twinning, together slowing the overall creep rate.
drafts.material_initial_state: A protective coating with an as-deposited dual-phase microstructure consisting of an FCC matrix containing dispersed BCC precipitates along with well-defined FCC/BCC interphase boundaries.
drafts.intervention: Tailor processing conditions (e.g., cooling rate, alloying additions) to systematically increase the volume fraction and refine the distribution of BCC precipitates within the FCC matrix.
drafts.conditions: Continuous uniaxial loading at elevated service temperatures (below the threshold for phase instability, for example <800°C) that mimic actual protective coating service conditions.
drafts.structural_mediator: The FCC/BCC interphase boundaries decorated with dynamic BCC precipitates that serve as obstacles to dislocation motion.
drafts.mechanism: BCC precipitates at the interphase boundaries inhibit dislocation climb and diffusion creep by acting as physical barriers, while the more ductile and twinning-capable FCC matrix primarily absorbs plastic strain. This synergy raises the effective stress required for creep and reduces the creep rate overall.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Coatings with a higher and more uniform BCC precipitate fraction will exhibit lower creep strain rates and higher stress exponents compared to coatings with a lower BCC fraction. Relative to the initial unmodified state, the upgraded microstructure should display delayed onset of significant plastic deformation under sustained loading.
drafts.baseline: A coating with a standard dual-phase microstructure where the BCC precipitate fraction and distribution are not optimized, showing higher creep strain rates and lower stress exponents.
drafts.boundary: This mechanism should hold under sustained mechanical loading and service temperatures where the phase stability is maintained (i.e., within the temperature range where no significant phase transformation occurs, such as below approximately 800°C).

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate a series of dual-phase HEA protective coatings with systematically varied BCC precipitate fractions and distributions. Subject all samples to continuous creep testing at a controlled elevated temperature (<800°C) under identical stress conditions while simultaneously performing in situ digital image correlation and post-mortem electron microscopy to track dislocation activity and microstructural evolution.
measurements: Creep strain rate vs. time under constant load
Stress exponent derived from creep curves
Quantitative analysis of BCC precipitate fraction and spacing using microscopy
Dislocation density and interaction with interphase boundaries
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If an increase in the BCC precipitate fraction or improved interphase boundary characteristics does not lead to a measurable decrease in the creep strain rate (or a corresponding increase in the stress exponent) compared to the baseline sample, or if dislocations are observed to traverse the interphase boundaries unobstructed, the hypothesized mechanism would be refuted.
